sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — includes parts of the skull and lower jaws but lacks the tail and most foot bones.
This skeleton represents a subadult individual that had not yet reached full growth.
A distinctive feature is the jugal bone, which has a high front branch tapering into a sharp, needle-like point.
The shoulder blade is fan-like expanded toward the rear.
The pteroid bone is small and slender, shaped like an exclamation mark.
Amateur paleontologist Umberto Venier discovered the holotype skeleton in 1997 inside a boulder in the Seazza brook near Preone in the Dolomites.

Fabio Marco Dalla Vecchia formally named the genus and its type species, Seazzadactylus venieri, in 2019. The generic name combines the brook's name with the Greek word for 'finger', while the specific name honors the discoverer.
Seazzadactylus is classified as a basal pterosaur outside of the Monofenestrata clade.
Cladistic analysis places it in a clade with Arcticodactylus, Austriadraco, Carniadactylus, Raeticodactylus, and Caviramus, a group named Caviramidae in a 2020 study by Matthew G. Baron.
In the evolutionary tree, Seazzadactylus is positioned directly above Austriadraco and below Carniadactylus.
The species is classified within the unranked family Eopterosauria.

Seazzadactylus lived during the late Triassic, specifically the Norian stage between 219 and 214 million years ago, in what is now Italy, while other records suggest a broader time range for the Norian stage from 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago.
Other records suggest the time range for this animal is the Norian stage, from 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago.
